title: Simple Ideas to Be Credible in an AI-Addled World
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. offers five working-draft strategies for maintaining teacher Credibility with students around AI use, grounded in his Five Key Beliefs framework. The piece argues that AI temptation among students is structurally conditioned — by the difficulty of learning itself, endemic busywork, and over-pressured academic environments — making moral prohibition insufficient. Effective credibility requires naming the temptation honestly, delivering frequent mini-sermons about why learning matters, connecting those Value arguments to the specific harm that AI shortcutting causes, sharing the teacher's own positive AI use cases, and modeling productive AI use as AI-as-tutor rather than AI-as-work-machine.
points: Acknowledging the structural causes of AI temptation — hard work, busywork, over-pressure — signals student awareness and care, which are prerequisites for Credibility in this domain.
Mini-sermons, brief and frequent expressions of why a subject matters, are the vehicle for Value cultivation, which in turn makes the costs of AI shortcutting legible to students.
Teacher Credibility in the AI domain depends partly on authentic personal engagement: sharing how one uses AI to aid one's own learning, not bypass it, models the distinction being taught.
Showing students how to use AI as a quizzing partner — giving it a vocab list and asking it to quiz you — is a concrete, immediately actionable alternative to delegation of work.
Framing this article as working draft thinking models the intellectual honesty that Credibility requires: not claiming to have solved what remains genuinely unsettled.
quotes: Secondary students are tempted to use AI to shortcut the work of learning because 1) the work of learning is hard, 2) most secondary students still receive way too much busywork in school, or 3) they are over-pressured (which, in light of the Yerkes-Dodson Law, is always going to lead to diminished performance and poorer decision-making). Speaking to these realities signals that you care about students and you're aware of their reality.

Most teachers give students speeches from time to time about how awesome their subject is. No teacher gives students enough of these kinds of messages though, and many teachers who do give these messages make them overly long. This is where mini-sermons come in (Strategy #4 in The Will to Learn).

You've got to then take all that Value-cultivation you're doing with those mini-sermons and parlay it into how common student AI use cases are so harmful. Learning in all the subject areas is really good for lots of amazing reasons. But when you ask an AI to complete your homework for you or write the essay for you, you're missing out on all that goodness.

It's very helpful to be acquainted with the tools yourself. Share positive use cases from your own life — situations where you're using it in a way that aids your learning without doing the hard work for you.

My go-to example here is giving an AI a study guide or a vocab list and asking it to quiz you. The tools are getting better and better at knowing how to help students learn (like a tutor) versus acting like mindless work completion machines.
